questions.question: Describe how water circulation influence hydrocarbon migration. / [CO1]

  • • Moving hydrocarbons from source rocks towards reservoir rocks by pushing them along pressure gradients.
  • • Deflecting or redirecting hydrocarbon movement from purely buoyancy-driven vertical migration to more
  • lateral or complex path.
  • • Strong water flow can either help trap hydrocarbons by sealing them against barriers or cause leakage by
  • flushing hydrocarbons out of reservoirs. (Any three significant points give full credits)

  • gas drilling is cooling and lubricating the drill bit to reduce wear and tear, carrying cuttings to the
  • surface to prevent clogging of the wellbore and also controlling formation pressure to prevent
  • blowouts. (Any three points 3 Marks)

questions.question: Illustrate the softening point test of bitumen. / [CO6] [3x4 = 12]
questions.solution_html:
• Illustrate the softening point test of bitumen. [An] / [CO6]
  • The ring and ball method: The apparatus needed for the test is ring and ball apparatus. The material being
  • tested is heated to (75 – 100℃) above its softening point and stirred until it becomes liquid. The brass rings
  • are heated near to the temperature equivalent to molten material and placed on a metal plate coated with dextrin
  • and glycerin. The test material is placed on the ring and allowed to cool for 30 minutes. Excess material is
  • removed with the help of a knife. Assemble the apparatus with the rings, thermometer and ball guid es in
  • position. Fill the bath with distilled water to a height of 50 mm above the upper surface of the rings. The
  • starting temperature should be 5℃. Apply heat to the bath and stir the liquid so that the temperature rises at a
  • uniform rate of 5 ± 0.5℃ per minute. With the increase in temperature of the bath the bitumen material softens
  • up and the steel balls start to sink and carry a portion of material with it. The temperature is noted down when
  • any of the steel balls touches the bottom plate. (Correct procedure gives 3 marks)

questions.question: Explain the principle of the Abel flash point test. / [CO6] [3x4 = 12]

  • give off enough vapour to ignite momentarily in the presence of a flame. In this method, the oil
  • sample is heated slowly in a closed cup apparatus, and a smal l test flame is introduced at regular
  • temperature intervals. The temperature at which a brief flash appears is recorded as the flash point
  • of the oil.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the environmental risks of transporting oil and gas by pipeline versus by tanker (ship). / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare and contrast the environmental risks of transporting oil and gas by pipeline versus
  • by tanker (ship). [U]/[CO2]
  • Pipelines are commonly used for transporting oil and gas over long distances on land and
  • underwater. Pipelines are usually safer and more energy -efficient for continuous transport, but
  • leaks may go unnoticed for long periods and affect land ecosystems. Pip eline accidents are
  • generally localized . The main environmental risk is leakage caused by corrosion, equipment
  • failure, or accidental damage. Pipeline leaks can contaminate soil, groundwater, rivers, and
  • agricultural land. Gas pipeline leaks may also relea se methane, a harmful greenhouse gas.
  • However, pipelines generally have lower accident rates and produce less air pollution during
  • normal operation.
  • Tankers are mainly used for transporting crude oil and liquefied natural gas across oceans.
  • Tankers can transport large quantities internationally, but accidents may cause sudden and
  • catastrophic marine pollution. The major environmental risk is oil spills caused by collisions,
  • grounding, storms, or equipment failure. Large oil spills can severely damage marine ecosystems,
  • kill fish and birds, and pollute coastlines for many years. Tankers also contribute to air pollution
  • through fuel emissions and may introduce invasive species through ballast water discharge. Tanker
  • spills can spread over vast ocean areas and have long-lasting environmental effects.
  • (3.5 marks each for Pipeline and Tankers)

questions.question: Explain the composition, functions and properties of Light Diesel Oil and Lubricating oil. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the composition, functions and properties of Light Diesel Oil and Lubricating oil.
  • [U]/[CO4]
  • Light Diesel Oil (LDO): Composition: Light Diesel Oil is a middle distillate petroleum product
  • obtained during crude oil refining. It mainly contains hydrocarbons such as paraffins, naphthenes,
  • and aromatic compounds with carbon numbers generally ranging from C10 to C20.
  • Functions
  • • Used as fuel in diesel engines, boilers, furnaces, and generators.
  • • Provides energy for industrial heating and power generation.
  • • Used in agricultural pumps and heavy machinery.
  • Properties
  • • Moderate viscosity and good flow characteristics.
  • • High calorific value and good combustion efficiency.
  • • Higher flash point than petrol, making it safer to handle.
  • • Low volatility and good storage stability.
  • Lubricating Oil: Composition: Lubricating oil is produced from heavy fractions of crude oil and
  • contains high molecular weight hydrocarbons along with additives such as antioxidants,
  • detergents, anti-wear agents, and corrosion inhibitors.
  • Functions
  • • Reduces friction and wear between moving machine parts.
  • • Helps in cooling engine components by removing heat.
  • • Prevents corrosion and rust formation.
  • • Cleans engine parts by carrying away dirt and metal particles.
  • • Provides sealing between moving parts.
  • Properties
  • • High viscosity and good viscosity index.
  • • High boiling point and low volatility.
  • • Good thermal and oxidation stability.
  • • Non-corrosive and resistant to foaming.

questions.question: Compare and contrast Natural Rubber Modified Bitumen and Bitumen Emulsion in terms of performance, durability, and environmental impact. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare and contrast Natural Rubber Modified Bitumen and Bitumen Emulsion in terms of performance,
  • durability, and environmental impact. [An] / [CO4]
  • Performance
  • • NRMB is designed for higher performance in terms of flexibility, el asticity, and resistance to extreme
  • temperatures. The natural rubber modification improves the high -temperature stability and low -temperature
  • flexibility of bitumen, making it suitable for regions with temperature fluctuations and high traffic volumes.
  • • It offers better resistance to cracking under temperature changes and deformations from heavy traffic,
  • enhancing the overall structural integrity of the road.
  • • NRMB improves skid resistance, making it safer for driving, especially in wet or icy conditions due to the
  • rubber's grip-enhancing properties.
  • • Bitumen emulsion is a water -based suspension of bitumen, making it easier to handle and apply at lower
  • temperatures than conventional bitumen. It is generally used for surface treatments and patching work rather
  • than heavy-duty applications like road paving.
  • • While it performs well for surface dressing (coating aggregates for road surfaces), it does not provide the same
  • long-term structural benefits as NRMB. Bitumen emulsion has lower temperature stability and is not as flexible
  • as NRMB in handling high thermal or traffic stresses.
  • • Bitumen emulsions are used in lower temperatures (usually between 20°C to 60°C) compared to conventional
  • hot bitumen. They are sprayed onto surfaces or mixed with aggregates.
  • • The emulsion breaks once applied, with the water evaporating and leaving behind the bitumen to bind the
  • aggregate or surface.
  • Durability & Environmental Impact
  • • NRMB is considered more environmentally friendly in some aspects because it often uses recycled rubber
  • from tires, reducing the amount of rubber waste that ends up in landfills. This helps promote sustainability in
  • road construction.
  • • The durability of NRM B reduces the frequency of road repairs, which in turn decreases the environmental
  • footprint over time due to fewer construction activities and material usage.
  • • Bitumen emulsion is also considered environmentally friendly because it requires less energy to produce and
  • apply compared to hot bitumen. Since it is water-based, it has lower emissions during the application process,
  • making it safer for workers and the environment.
  • (Any one point each for performance, durability, and environmental impact of NRMB & BE give 7 marks)

questions.question: Describe the working principle of atmospheric and vacuum distillation. Compare their fraction seperated and applications. / [CO6]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the working principle of atmospheric and vacuum distillation. Compare their faction
  • separated and applications. [U]/ [CO6]
  • Atmospheric distillation and vacuum distillation are important refining processes used to separate
  • crude oil into different fractions based on their boiling points.
  • In atmospheric distillation, crude oil is first heated in a furnace to about 350 –400°C and
  • then introduced into a distillation column operating at atmospheric pressure. As the vapours rise
  • through the column, components with different boiling points conden se at different heights and
  • are collected separately.
  • Fractions Separated
  • • Petroleum gas, Naphtha, Gasoline (petrol), Kerosene, Diesel, Heavy gas oil, Residue
  • Applications
  • • Production of fuels such as petrol, diesel, and kerosene.
  • • Provides feedstock for further refining processes like catalytic cracking and reforming.
  • Vacuum distillation is used for the heavy residue obtained from atmospheric distillation. The
  • process is carried out under reduced pressure, which lowers the boiling points of heavy
  • hydrocarbons and prevents thermal cracking or decomposition at high temperatures.
  • Fractions Separated
  • • Vacuum gas oil, Lubricating oil fractions, Paraffin wax, Asphalt or bitumen residue
  • Applications
  • • Production of lubricating oils, waxes, and bitumen.
  • • Provides feedstock for catalytic cracking and other secondary refining processes.
  • (Working principle 1.5 marks and 1 mark each for faction separated and applications
  • for each distillation method)

questions.solution_html:
• Explain the procedure and significance of the penetration test for bitumen. [U]/[CO6]
  • The penetration test is a standard test used to determine the hardness or consistency of bitumen. It
  • measures the depth to which a standard needle penetrates the bitumen sample under specified
  • conditions.
  • Procedure: The bitumen sample is heated and poured into a standard container, then allowed to
  • cool. The sample is maintained at a standard temperature of 25°C. A standard needle loaded with
  • a weight of 100 g is placed just touching the surface of the bitumen. The needle is allowed to
  • penetrate the sample freely for 5 seconds. The depth of penetration is measured in tenths of a
  • millimetre (dmm). The average value from repeated tests is reported as the penetration value of
  • the bitumen.
  • Significance of the Penetration Test
  • • It indicates the hardness or softness of bitumen.
  • • Helps in grading bitumen for different climatic and traffic conditions.
  • • Softer bitumen with higher penetration values is suitable for cold climates, while harder
  • bitumen with lower penetration values is suitable for hot climates.
  • • Ensures uniform quality and proper selection of bitumen for road construction.
  • • Assists in predicting the performance and durability of pavement materials.
  • Thus, the penetration test is an important quality control test used to classify bitumen and
  • determine its suitability for various engineering applications.
  • (Procedure and any three points of significance 3.5 marks each)
